title: AWS shared credentials file: secret values across profiles and file types
summary: A synthetic AWS credentials file with a [default] and a [user1] profile (a secret access key each, a session token in the second), and a config file profile that holds a secret access key inline.
rationale: One file carries several profiles, each its own credential, and the AWS CLI also reads credentials from the config file, so the same setting can appear in either file under a differently written section header ([user1] versus [profile user1]). The key ids sit on the line above each secret and are not part of the secret.

expectation.rationale: Flag the aws_secret_access_key values and the aws_session_token value. The AWS CLI page describes aws_secret_access_key as the secret key used as part of the credentials to authenticate, aws_session_token as part of manually specified temporary credentials, and says both can be stored in the config file though the credentials file is recommended. The access key id values are companion spans in the credentials-file fixture (acceptable to report, not required): their treatment as secrets is the existing aws:iam-user-access-key review, not asserted here (ADR 0021). Secret values are synthetic 40-character strings from the secret-key alphabet and were never issued.

sources.supports: aws_secret_access_key: Specifies the AWS secret key used as part of the credentials to authenticate the command request. Although this can be stored in the config file, we recommend that you store this in the credentials file.
aws_session_token: Specifies an AWS session token. A session token is required only if you manually specify temporary security credentials.
